summary: Most space games are just flight simulators, but AstroForge focuses on the hardest part of actually getting off the ground: the engineering trade-offs. We designed this project to completely kill the idea of a "perfect" spacecraft. Guided seamlessly through a 7-step mission cycle that mirrors real NASA problem-solving, players quickly realize they can't have it all. Whether you are trying to outrun a scorching 430°C Mercury sunrise or drill into a freezing lunar crater, surviving the launch means balancing hard numbers across Mass, Power, Budget, and Time to make smart sacrifices at every turn. Alongside the built-in game guidelines that help you along the way, we also included an advanced knowledge base as a side platform for players who want to dive deeper into the real aerospace mechanics behind their choices. While AstroForge is currently built as a single-player prototype, we are laying the groundwork for a multiplayer expansion where players will eventually take on conflicting NASA roles—like a budget-stressed Project Manager and a weight-obsessed Lead Engineer—forcing them to actively argue and negotiate these compromises together. It steps away from basic STEM trivia to show what space exploration is really about: it takes more than just big rockets to succeed, it takes tough choices.
details:
Project Title: Astro Forge

Don't just fly the ship. Engineer the mission.

The Inspiration

Most space simulators on the market share the same flaw where they give you an unlimited budget, infinite power, and let you build a "perfect" spacecraft just to see if you can fly it. But if you talk to any real aerospace engineer, they will tell you the truth that space exploration is not about having everything you want. It is about the brutal reality of the engineering trade-off.

We built AstroForge because we wanted to capture the hardest, most intense part of a NASA mission: The Design Lab. We wanted to create an experience that kills the illusion of the "perfect ship" and forces players to make the exact same agonizing compromises real flight controllers make every day.

What is AstroForge?

AstroForge is a platform that allow players to work through a realistic 7-step mission cycle that mirrors actual NASA problem-solving. Players select a scenario (like outrunning a 430°C Mercury sunrise), choose a vehicle type, and enter the Design Lab. Here, they must equip their spacecraft with thermal plating, batteries, and scientific tools. However, every single part added affects global stats. Surviving the launch means actively balancing hard numbers across four strict limits: Mass, Power, Budget, and Time. If your rover is too heavy, you get caught by the sun and melt; if you strip away instruments to gain speed, the mission fails its scientific objective.

How does it work?

1. Prototype Overview

- AstroForge is built around a structured problem-solving loop rather than an open sandbox. The core gameplay consists of a 7-step mission cycle from defining the objective to the final debrief and redesign.

2. The 7-Steps Mission Cycle

2.1 Define the Objective

- Players select a real-world scenario.

- Players go through its details and understand it.

- Players select a priority.

- Players cannot achieve every objective at once. Trying to do so will result in mission failure, teaching them that every mission requires trade-offs and prioritisation.

2.2 Mission Approach

- Players need to select the correct approach to proceed.

- Inappropriate approach will lead to game over and explanation will be given.

2.3 & 2.4 The Design Lab + Trade - off Matrix

- The core of the game, where players equip their spacecraft with components based on their chosen priorities.

- The Engineering HUB bar will change according to the componets selected.

- Every component you add directly affects your spacecraft's overall stats. Add a heavy drill? Your mass limit goes into the red. Switch to a nuclear battery? Your budget takes a hit.

- A step-by-step guide for the first mission to help players understand what they need to do.

2.5 Pre-Launch Diagnostics

- In our prototype, the Pre-Launch Diagnostics screen demonstrates how the game will evaluate a spacecraft before launch. It features a final checklist covering key parameters such as Mass, Power, Budget, and Risk, all of which must meet the mission requirements to ensure a safe launch. For now, we use interactive UI states to demonstrate a successful test run. Our next priority is to develop the mathematical backend that dynamically calculates these values based on the components selected by players.

2.6 Launch & Survive

- In the "Launch & Survive" phase, players follow their mission through a day-by-day Mission Log, tracking everything from liftoff to planetary landing and surface operations. Instead of simply receiving a pass or fail result, players experience how their spacecraft performs throughout the mission. They must also make critical decisions along the way, such as selecting a landing site on Mercury, while dealing with environmental hazards like extreme solar heat. Once the spacecraft successfully collects its data, a final mission report is generated for debriefing.

2.7 Debrief & Redesign

- The final stage is the Mission Result & Evaluation dashboard, where players receive a detailed breakdown of their spacecraft's performance. Our prototype demonstrates how the game evaluates players based on metrics such as Mission Success/Failure, Scientific Findings, Resource Efficiency, and Risk Evaluation. The results are linked to the priorities set at the beginning of the mission, highlighting which design choices worked and where compromises led to failure. While our hackathon focused on developing this feedback experience, building the backend algorithm to automatically calculate scores based on the components selected in the Design Lab is a key goal for future development.

What benefits does it have?

AstroForge makes complex aerospace engineering highly accessible. Real aerospace math is intimidating, so we designed the learning curve to be entirely frictionless. Players don't need a physics degree to play; dynamic, in-game guidelines pop up to explain why a battery is draining too fast or why a rover is too heavy, teaching the physics naturally as part of the gameplay loop. Additionally, we built an advanced Knowledge Base as a side platform. It doesn't interrupt the game, but allows curious players to dive deeper into real-world NASA facts, component blueprints, and planetary science at their own pace.

What is the intended impact of the project?

We took what might seem like the most tedious parts of space exploration—budgeting, weight limits, and resource management. We turned them into an exciting, high-stakes experience. Rather than simply exploring the vastness of space, players face real environmental challenges, such as outrunning the rising sunlight on Mercury or searching for water ice in the freezing, pitch-dark craters of the Lunar South Pole. By turning engineering trade-offs into gameplay, AstroForge brings a fresh perspective to the space simulation genre.

Our creativity also extends to how we built the game. Instead of relying on pre-made templates, we designed every page and interface by scratch. We wanted aerospace engineering to feel less intimidating, so we created a clean, user-friendly interface that welcomes both young explorers and casual players. We also integrated helpful in-game guidelines to support players along the way, together with a dedicated Knowledge Base where they can independently explore real-world aerospace facts and planetary science.

What factors did your team consider?

Balancing Fun and Realism: We wanted constraints like Mass, Power, and Budget to feel challenging without making the game impossible. We also focused on presenting these numbers visually so players could immediately understand the consequences of their decisions.

Accessibility: We kept the Knowledge Base separate from the main gameplay to avoid overwhelming new players with too much information. This allows them to learn through experience and explore deeper knowledge whenever they want.

Future Multiplayer Dynamics: Although our current prototype focuses on single-player gameplay, we also considered its potential for multiplayer expansion. In the future, players could take on different NASA roles, such as a budget-conscious Project Manager and a weight-focused Lead Engineer, creating fun debates and teamwork as they work towards a shared mission.
